s.line: She was awakened by a shock,

w: הָיְתָה שׁוֹכֶבֶת|had been lying|pa'al ptc · שׁ־כ־ב
s.line: so sudden and severe that if Dorothy had not been lying on the soft bed she might have been hurt.
s.note: אִם … הָיְתָה שׁוֹכֶבֶת … הִיא הָיְתָה עֲלוּלָה: for an unreal condition ("if she had not been lying …, she might have …") everyday Hebrew uses הָיָה + present participle in both halves. עָלוּל = liable to, used for bad outcomes: עָלוּל לָרֶדֶת גֶּשֶׁם (it may rain). נִפְגַּע (nif'al) = was hurt, the passive of פָּגַע (to hit, to hurt). On the news: שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים נִפְגְּעוּ = two people were injured.

s.line: As it was, the jar made her catch her breath and wonder what had happened;
s.note: עָצַר לָהּ אֶת הַנְּשִׁימָה: "stopped to her the breath". Hebrew often marks whose body part with לְ + pronoun instead of a possessive: כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ (my head hurts). תָּהָה = to wonder, a bookish verb; in speech you'd hear שָׁאֲלָה אֶת עַצְמָהּ.

s.line: and Toto put his cold little nose into her face and whined dismally.
Dorothy sat up and noticed that the house was not moving;
s.note: שָׂם לֵב ("put heart") = to notice, pay attention, one of the most common Hebrew idioms: לֹא שַׂמְתִּי לֵב (I didn't notice). הִתְיַשֵּׁב (hitpa'el) = to sit down or sit up, from the same root as יָשַׁב (to sit).

s.line: nor was it dark, for the bright sunshine came in at the window, flooding the little room.
s.note: הֵצִיף (hif'il) = to flood something; צָף (pa'al) = to float. You'll hear הֵצִיפוּ אוֹתִי בַּעֲבוֹדָה = they swamped me with work.

w: בְּעִקְּבוֹתֶיהָ|on her heels|~lit. in her footsteps
s.line: She sprang from her bed and with Toto at her heels ran and opened the door.
s.note: בְּעִקְּבוֹת = "in the footsteps of, following". In the news it means "following, as a result of": בְּעִקְּבוֹת הַהַחְלָטָה (following the decision). Careful with רָצָה: here it is "she ran" (root ר־ו־ץ), but the very same word, vowels and all, is also "he wanted" (root ר־צ־ה). "She wanted" is רָצְתָה.

s.line: The little girl gave a cry of amazement and looked about her,
s.note: פָּלַט = to let out, blurt out (a cry, a word); in computing פֶּלֶט is "output". תַּדְהֵמָה (amazement) shares a root with מַדְהִים (amazing).

w: הָלְכוּ וְגָדְלוּ|grew bigger and bigger|~idiom: went and grew
s.line: her eyes growing bigger and bigger at the wonderful sights she saw.
s.note: הָלַךְ וְ… + a second verb = "more and more": הַמַּצָּב הוֹלֵךְ וּמִשְׁתַּפֵּר (the situation keeps improving). מַרְאֶה (sight, view) is masculine even though its plural is מַרְאוֹת, so the adjective is נִפְלָאִים.

s.line: The cyclone had set the house down very gently—for a cyclone—in the midst of a country of marvelous beauty.
s.note: הִנִּיחַ (hif'il) = to put down, place. It also means "to assume": אֲנִי מַנִּיחַ שֶׁ… (I assume that …). יַחֲסִית לְ… = "relatively, for a …": חַם יַחֲסִית לְחֹרֶף (warm for winter).

s.line: There were lovely patches of greensward all about, with stately trees bearing rich and luscious fruits.
s.note: מַרְשִׁים (impressive) is a hif'il participle: הִרְשִׁים = to impress, and רֹשֶׁם = an impression. חֶלְקָה (a plot of land) comes from חֵלֶק (part).

s.line: Banks of gorgeous flowers were on every hand,
and birds with rare and brilliant plumage sang and fluttered in the trees and bushes.
s.note: צִפּוֹר is feminine, so "having" is בַּעֲלוֹת, the feminine plural of בַּעַל. פִּרְפֵּר = to flutter, flap about; a fish out of water מְפַרְפֵּר too. פַּרְפַּר = butterfly.

s.line: A little way off was a small brook, rushing and sparkling along between green banks,
s.note: זָרַם = to flow; זֶרֶם = a current, and also electric current: אֵין זֶרֶם (there's no power). גָּדָה = river bank; הַגָּדָה הַמַּעֲרָבִית is the West Bank.

s.line: and murmuring in a voice very grateful to a little girl who had lived so long on the dry, gray prairies.
s.note: Baum's "grateful" here is old English for "pleasing", so Hebrew says נָעִים. כֹּה = "so", a more literary word for כָּל כָּךְ. פִּכְפֵּךְ is the classic Hebrew verb for the sound of a brook.

s.line: While she stood looking eagerly at the strange and beautiful sights, she noticed coming toward her a group of the queerest people she had ever seen.
s.note: בְּעוֹד = "while", and it takes the present tense even in a story told in the past: בְּעוֹד הִיא עוֹמֶדֶת = while she stood. הִבְחִין בְּ… (hif'il) = to notice, a little more formal than שָׂם לֵב לְ…; note the preposition בְּ.

s.line: They were not as big as the grown folk she had always been used to;
s.note: מְבֻגָּר = adult, grown-up, a pu'al participle used as a noun, like מְאֻשָּׁר. מְבֻגָּר מִ… = older than. רָגִיל לְ… = used to …; on its own רָגִיל = ordinary, regular.

s.line: but neither were they very small.
In fact, they seemed about as tall as Dorothy, who was a well-grown child for her age,
s.note: מְפֻתַּחַת לְגִילָהּ = "well developed for her age", exactly what Israelis say about a child. מְפֻתָּח is the pu'al participle of פִּתֵּחַ (to develop); מְדִינָה מְפֻתַּחַת = a developed country. לְמַעֲשֶׂה = in fact, actually.

s.line: although they were, so far as looks go, many years older.
Three were men and one a woman, and all were oddly dressed.
s.note: לָבוּשׁ (dressed) is a pa'ul participle of לָבַשׁ (to put on, wear). בְּאֹפֶן + adjective is a common way to make an adverb: בְּאֹפֶן מוּזָר = strangely, בְּאֹפֶן אִישִׁי = personally.

s.line: They wore round hats that rose to a small point a foot above their heads,
s.note: Hebrew has a different verb of "wearing" for each item: לָבַשׁ clothes, חָבַשׁ a hat, נָעַל shoes, עָנַד jewelry or a watch, הִרְכִּיב glasses. In speech many people simply say שָׂם כּוֹבַע. A foot is about thirty centimeters, so כִּשְׁלוֹשִׁים ("about thirty") with כְּ = approximately.

s.line: with little bells around the brims that tinkled sweetly as they moved.
s.note: צִלְצֵל = to ring; it is also the everyday verb for phoning: צִלְצַלְתִּי אֵלֶיךָ (I called you). שׁוּלַיִם = edges, margins, the brim of a hat: בְּשׁוּלֵי הָעִיר = on the outskirts of town.

s.line: The hats of the men were blue;
the little woman’s hat was white,
and she wore a white gown that hung in pleats from her shoulders.
Over it were sprinkled little stars that glistened in the sun like diamonds.
s.note: מְפֻזָּר is a pu'al participle: פִּזֵּר (pi'el) = to scatter, sprinkle → מְפֻזָּר = scattered. Of a person, מְפֻזָּר means scatterbrained: הוּא קְצָת מְפֻזָּר.

s.line: The men were dressed in blue, of the same shade as their hats,
and wore well-polished boots with a deep roll of blue at the tops.
s.note: מְצֻחְצָח (polished) is pu'al: צִחְצֵחַ = to polish, and it is also the verb for brushing teeth: לְצַחְצֵחַ שִׁנַּיִם. מַגָּפַיִם is a dual, like נַעֲלַיִם (shoes).

s.line: The men, Dorothy thought, were about as old as Uncle Henry, for two of them had beards.
s.note: זָקָן (beard) and זָקֵן (old) have the same letters, זקן; only the last vowel differs. The next sentence uses the second one: זְקֵנָה = old (fem.). בְּגִילוֹ שֶׁל = "at the age of", the same pattern as אִשְׁתּוֹ שֶׁל.

s.line: But the little woman was doubtless much older.
Her face was covered with wrinkles, her hair was nearly white, and she walked rather stiffly.
s.note: פָּנִים (face) is grammatically plural, so it takes הָיוּ and the plural מְכֻסִּים: הַפָּנִים שֶׁלּוֹ אֲדֻמִּים (his face is red). מְכֻסֶּה is the pu'al participle of כִּסָּה (to cover). בְּצוּרָה + adjective works like בְּאֹפֶן, and the adjective is feminine because צוּרָה is.

s.line: When these people drew near the house where Dorothy was standing in the doorway, they paused and whispered among themselves, as if afraid to come farther.
s.note: הִתְלַחֲשׁוּ: hitpa'el often means doing something to each other: לָחַשׁ = to whisper, הִתְלַחֵשׁ = to whisper together; likewise הִתְכַּתֵּב = to correspond. שֶׁדּוֹרוֹתִי עָמְדָה בַּפֶּתַח שֶׁלּוֹ: "that Dorothy stood in its doorway". A relative clause in Hebrew often repeats the noun as a pronoun (שֶׁלּוֹ = of it).

s.line: But the little old woman walked up to Dorothy, made a low bow and said, in a sweet voice:
s.note: נִגַּשׁ אֶל = to approach, go up to; it is nif'al in form but active in meaning. From the same root: נָגִישׁ = accessible. קָדָה קִידָה, as in קָד קִידָה.

w: בְּרוּכָה הַבָּאָה|welcome|~idiom: blessed is she who comes
s.line: “You are welcome, most noble Sorceress, to the land of the Munchkins.
s.note: בְּרוּכָה הַבָּאָה = welcome (to a woman). To a man בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא, to a group בְּרוּכִים הַבָּאִים, which you see on signs everywhere. "Sorceress" here is קוֹסֶמֶת, the feminine of קוֹסֵם (wizard, magician).

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: We are so grateful to you for having killed the Wicked Witch of the East,
s.note: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה (fem. אֲסִירַת תּוֹדָה, pl. אֲסִירֵי תּוֹדָה) = "a prisoner of thanks", the standard phrase for "deeply grateful". אָסִיר alone = a prisoner. עַל שֶׁ… + past = "for having …": תּוֹדָה עַל שֶׁבָּאתָ (thanks for coming).

s.line: and for setting our people free from bondage.”
s.note: שִׁחְרֵר (pi'el, four-letter root) = to set free, release; שִׁחְרוּר = liberation, also discharge from the army. עַבְדוּת (slavery) comes from עֶבֶד (slave), as in the Passover phrase מֵעַבְדוּת לְחֵרוּת (from slavery to freedom).

s.line: Dorothy listened to this speech with wonder.
s.note: הִקְשִׁיב לְ… = to listen to; note the לְ. שָׁמַע is to hear, הִקְשִׁיב is to pay attention with your ears. דְּבָרִים = words or things, so הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה = what was said.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: What could the little woman possibly mean by calling her a sorceress, and saying she had killed the Wicked Witch of the East?
s.note: הִתְכַּוֵּן לְ… = to mean, to intend: לְמָה אַתָּה מִתְכַּוֵּן? = what do you mean? לֹא הִתְכַּוַּנְתִּי = I didn't mean it. קָרָא לְ… + a name = to call someone something.

s.line: Dorothy was an innocent, harmless little girl, who had been carried by a cyclone many miles from home;
s.note: Hebrew turns "who had been carried by a cyclone" into an active clause: שֶׁטּוֹרְנָדוֹ נָשָׂא אוֹתָהּ ("that a cyclone carried her"). מַזִּיק (hif'il participle of הִזִּיק, to harm) = harmful; as a noun it means a pest.

s.line: and she had never killed anything in all her life.
But the little woman evidently expected her to answer;
s.note: צִפָּה לְ… (pi'el) = to expect, look forward to: אֲנִי מְצַפֶּה לִשְׁמֹעַ מִמְּךָ (I look forward to hearing from you). Inside "it was clear that …" Hebrew keeps the present מְצַפָּה.

s.line: so Dorothy said, with hesitation,
“You are very kind, but there must be some mistake.
s.note: בֶּטַח = surely, probably; on its own as an answer it means "sure!". כָּלְשֶׁהוּ / כָּלְשֶׁהִי = some, any (after the noun); in speech you'd also hear אֵיזוֹשֶׁהִי טָעוּת.

s.line: I have not killed anything.”
“Your house did, anyway,” replied the little old woman, with a laugh, “and that is the same thing.
s.note: כֵּן before a verb is emphatic, like English "did" in "your house did": it answers a denial. הוּא לֹא בָּא? – הוּא כֵּן בָּא! (He didn't come? He did come!). בְּכָל מִקְרֶה = anyway, in any case.

s.line: See!” she continued, pointing to the corner of the house.
s.note: תִּרְאִי is future in form ("you will see"), but spoken Hebrew uses the future as a softer imperative: תַּגִּיד לִי (tell me), תִּשְׁמַע (listen). הִצְבִּיעַ עַל = to point at; הִצְבִּיעַ alone = to vote (or raise a hand in class).

s.line: “There are her two feet, still sticking out from under a block of wood.”
s.note: בּוֹלֵט = sticking out, prominent; בּוֹלֵט לָעַיִן = conspicuous. רֶגֶל is feminine, so "two" is שְׁתֵּי and the participle is בּוֹלְטוֹת. רַגְלַיִם covers both "legs" and "feet".

s.line: Dorothy looked, and gave a little cry of fright.
There, indeed, just under the corner of the great beam the house rested on, two feet were sticking out,
s.note: אָכֵן = indeed, sure enough, a slightly formal word common in writing and the news. נִשְׁעַן עַל = to lean on, rest on (nif'al, active meaning); מִשְׁעֶנֶת = the back of a chair. מַמָּשׁ = right, really: מַמָּשׁ פֹּה (right here).

s.line: shod in silver shoes with pointed toes.
s.note: נָעוּל = wearing shoes, from נָעַל (to put on shoes). The same verb means "to lock", so הַדֶּלֶת נְעוּלָה = the door is locked. נַעַל (shoe) comes from this root. חַרְטוֹם = beak, the bow of a ship, the toe of a shoe.

w: אוֹי וַאֲבוֹי|oh dear|~idiom: woe and alas
וְסָפְקָה כַּפַּיִם|and wrung her hands|~idiom: clapped palms
s.line: “Oh, dear! Oh, dear!” cried Dorothy, clasping her hands together in dismay.
s.note: אוֹי וַאֲבוֹי is a common exclamation of dismay, used both seriously and jokingly: אוֹי וַאֲבוֹי לָנוּ (woe is us). סָפַק כַּפַּיִם = to clasp or wring one's hands in distress, a set phrase from the Bible still used in writing. בֶּהָלָה = alarm, panic; נִבְהַל is from the same root.

s.line: “The house must have fallen on her.
s.note: כַּנִּרְאֶה = apparently, probably, from נִרְאֶה (seems). Hebrew uses an adverb where English says "must have …".

s.line: Whatever shall we do?”
s.note: נַעֲשֶׂה = "we will do". With one vowel changed, נַעֲשָׂה is nif'al: "was done, became". Both are written נעשה without vowels, so מָה נַעֲשָׂה? would mean "what was done?".

w: אֵין מָה לַעֲשׂוֹת|there's nothing to be done|~idiom
s.line: “There is nothing to be done,” said the little woman calmly.
s.note: אֵין מָה לַעֲשׂוֹת = "there's nothing to do (about it)", what Israelis say with a shrug. The pattern אֵין מָה + infinitive is very common: אֵין מָה לְדַבֵּר (no need to discuss it), אֵין מָה לְהַפְסִיד (nothing to lose).

s.line: “But who was she?” asked Dorothy.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: “She was the Wicked Witch of the East, as I said,” answered the little woman.
“She has held all the Munchkins in bondage for many years,
s.note: הֶחֱזִיק (hif'il) = to hold, keep; תַּחְזִיק = hold this. It shares a root with חָזָק (strong). A length of time needs no preposition: שָׁנִים רַבּוֹת = for many years.

s.line: making them slave for her night and day.
s.note: הִכְרִיחַ = to force: אַף אֶחָד לֹא מַכְרִיחַ אוֹתְךָ (nobody's forcing you). הֶכְרֵחַ = necessity. יוֹם וָלַיְלָה is a fixed pair with the old וָ form of "and", like שָׁנָה וָחֵצִי (a year and a half).

s.line: Now they are all set free, and are grateful to you for the favor.”
s.note: מְשֻׁחְרָר is the pu'al participle of שִׁחְרֵר: set free, released; a חַיָּל מְשֻׁחְרָר is a discharged soldier. טוֹבָה = a favor: תַּעֲשֶׂה לִי טוֹבָה = do me a favor (often sarcastic).

s.line: “Who are the Munchkins?” inquired Dorothy.
s.note: הִתְעַנְיֵן = to be interested, and also to ask, inquire. הִתְעַנְיֵן בְּ… = to be interested in; מְעַנְיֵן = interesting. All come from עִנְיָן (matter, interest).

s.line: “They are the people who live in this land of the East where the Wicked Witch ruled.”
s.note: שָׁלַט בְּ… = to rule, control. Today you'll also hear it for languages: הוּא שׁוֹלֵט בְּעִבְרִית = he is fluent in Hebrew. שַׁלָּט = remote control, שֶׁלֶט = a sign.

s.line: “Are you a Munchkin?” asked Dorothy.
“No, but I am their friend, although I live in the land of the North.
s.note: לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ… = although, the everyday word; אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ… means the same and is more formal. Without שֶׁ: לַמְרוֹת הַגֶּשֶׁם = despite the rain.

s.line: When they saw the Witch of the East was dead the Munchkins sent a swift messenger to me, and I came at once.
s.note: מֵתָה can be the adjective "dead" (fem.) or the verb "she died": the spelling and vowels are the same. שָׁלִיחַ = messenger, from שָׁלַח (to send). Today a שָׁלִיחַ is usually the delivery guy: הַשָּׁלִיחַ שֶׁל הַפִּיצָה.

s.line: I am the Witch of the North.”
“Oh, gracious!” cried Dorothy.
s.note: אֱלֹהִים אַדִּירִים! = "good heavens!", an everyday exclamation of shock; אַדִּיר = mighty, and in slang "awesome".

s.line: “Are you a real witch?”
“Yes, indeed,” answered the little woman.
“But I am a good witch, and the people love me.
I am not as powerful as the Wicked Witch was who ruled here,

w: הָיִיתִי מְשַׁחְרֶרֶת|I would have freed|pi'el ptc · שׁ־ח־ר־ר
s.line: or I should have set the people free myself.”
s.note: הָיִיתִי מְשַׁחְרֶרֶת = "I would have freed": הָיָה + participle again, as at the start of the chapter, here for something that did not happen. אַחֶרֶת = otherwise (literally "other", fem.). בְּעַצְמִי = by myself, myself.

s.line: “But I thought all witches were wicked,” said the girl, who was half frightened at facing a real witch.
s.note: מְפֻחָד (fem. מְפֻחֶדֶת) = scared, a pu'al participle; compare פָּחַד (to be afraid) and מַפְחִיד (scary). מִכָּךְ שֶׁ… = "from the fact that …", a useful link word.

s.line: “Oh, no, that is a great mistake.
There were only four witches in all the Land of Oz, and two of them, those who live in the North and the South, are good witches.
s.note: אַרְבַּע מְכַשֵּׁפוֹת: with a feminine noun the number has no final ה (compare אַרְבָּעָה קִירוֹת in chapter 1). Likewise שְׁתַּיִם מֵהֶן, "two of them" (fem.). הֵן here works as "are", linking subject and predicate.

s.line: I know this is true, for I am one of them myself, and cannot be mistaken.
s.note: טָעָה = to be mistaken, and טָעוּת = a mistake, from the same root. אִם אֲנִי לֹא טוֹעָה = if I'm not mistaken. Hebrew has no passive here: "to be mistaken" is the simple active לִטְעוֹת.

s.line: Those who dwelt in the East and the West were, indeed, wicked witches;
s.note: Compare שֶׁגָּרוּ (who lived, past) here with שֶׁגָּרוֹת (who live, present fem. pl.) two sentences back. The verb גָּר has the same form for "he lives" and "he lived"; the endings tell the rest.

s.line: but now that you have killed one of them, there is but one Wicked Witch in all the Land of Oz—the one who lives in the West.”
“But,” said Dorothy, after a moment’s thought, “Aunt Em has told me that the witches were all dead—years and years ago.”
s.note: סִפֵּר (pi'el) = to tell; סָפַר (pa'al) = to count. Same root, different binyan: סִפְּרָה לִי = she told me, סָפְרָה עַד שָׁלוֹשׁ = she counted to three. You'll see the second one later in this chapter. לִפְנֵי + time = "… ago": לִפְנֵי שָׁנָה (a year ago).

s.line: “Who is Aunt Em?” inquired the little old woman.
s.note: מִי זֹאת? = "who is she?": spoken Hebrew uses זֶה / זֹאת as "is": מִי זֶה? (who's that?), מָה זֶה? (what's that?).

s.line: “She is my aunt who lives in Kansas, where I came from.”

w: שְׁקוּעָה בְּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת|lost in thought|~idiom: sunk in thoughts
s.line: The Witch of the North seemed to think for a time, with her head bowed and her eyes upon the ground.
s.note: שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת = lost in thought; שָׁקַע = to sink, and שְׁקִיעָה = sunset. מֻרְכָּן is a hof'al participle, the passive of הִרְכִּין (to bow, lower the head): הִרְכִּינָה אֶת הָרֹאשׁ → הָרֹאשׁ מֻרְכָּן. כְּשֶׁ… + a noun and an adjective describes how someone was: "with her head bowed".

s.line: Then she looked up and said,
“I do not know where Kansas is, for I have never heard that country mentioned before.
s.note: נִמְצָא (nif'al of מָצָא, to find) = "is located", literally "is found": אֵיפֹה נִמְצֵאת הַתַּחֲנָה? (where is the station?). מֵעוֹלָם לֹא = never (in the past), a little more formal than אַף פַּעַם לֹא. הִזְכִּיר (hif'il of ז־כ־ר, the root of זָכַר, to remember) = to mention or to remind.

s.line: But tell me, is it a civilized country?”
s.note: מְתֻרְבָּת (fem. מְתֻרְבֶּתֶת) = civilized, cultured, a pu'al participle built from תַּרְבּוּת (culture). Of a person: תִּתְנַהֵג בְּצוּרָה מְתֻרְבֶּתֶת! = behave in a civilized way!

s.line: “Oh, yes,” replied Dorothy.
“Then that accounts for it.
s.note: הִסְבִּיר (hif'il) = to explain; הֶסְבֵּר = an explanation, and סָבִיר = reasonable, likely. זֶה מַסְבִּיר הַכֹּל = that explains everything.

s.line: In the civilized countries I believe there are no witches left, nor wizards, nor sorceresses, nor magicians.
s.note: אַשָּׁף is an old word for a magician or sorcerer. Today it mostly means a wizard at something, an expert: אַשַּׁף מַחְשְׁבִים (a computer whiz). הֶאֱמִין (hif'il) = to believe; אֱמוּנָה = faith, and אָמֵן = amen, from the same root.

s.line: But, you see, the Land of Oz has never been civilized, for we are cut off from all the rest of the world.
s.note: מְנֻתָּק = cut off, disconnected, the pu'al participle of נִתֵּק (to disconnect). You'll hear it about phone calls (הַשִּׂיחָה נִתְּקָה, the call was cut off) and about people out of touch: הוּא מְנֻתָּק מֵהַמְּצִיאוּת. אַתְּ מְבִינָה = "you see", as a filler in speech.

s.line: Therefore we still have witches and wizards amongst us.”
“Who are the wizards?” asked Dorothy.
“Oz himself is the Great Wizard,” answered the Witch, sinking her voice to a whisper.
s.note: הִנְמִיךְ (hif'il) = to lower, from נָמוּךְ (low, short): תַּנְמִיךְ אֶת הַמּוּזִיקָה (turn the music down). Its opposite is הִגְבִּיהַּ, from גָּבֹהַּ. עַצְמוֹ after a noun = "himself": הַמְּנַהֵל עַצְמוֹ (the manager himself).

s.line: “He is more powerful than all the rest of us together.
He lives in the City of Emeralds.”
Dorothy was going to ask another question,
s.note: עָמַד לְ… + infinitive = "to be about to …": הָרַכֶּבֶת עוֹמֶדֶת לָצֵאת (the train is about to leave). Without the infinitive עָמַד simply means "stood".

w: בְּקוֹל רָם|loudly|~lit. in a high voice
s.line: but just then the Munchkins, who had been standing silently by, gave a loud shout and pointed to the corner of the house where the Wicked Witch had been lying.
s.note: בְּקוֹל רָם = "in a high voice", meaning aloud, loudly: תִּקְרָא בְּקוֹל רָם (read it aloud). Hebrew has only one past tense, so שֶׁעָמְדוּ covers "who had been standing" and שָׁכְבָה covers "had been lying".

s.line: “What is it?” asked the little old woman, and looked, and began to laugh.

w: חוּץ מִנַּעֲלֵי הַכֶּסֶף|except the silver shoes
s.line: The feet of the dead Witch had disappeared entirely, and nothing was left but the silver shoes.
s.note: נֶעֱלַם = to disappear, nif'al with an active meaning, like נִשְׁאַר (to remain). The hif'il הֶעֱלִים = to make disappear, to hide. לֹא … כְּלוּם = nothing, the spoken partner of שׁוּם דָּבָר.

s.line: “She was so old,” explained the Witch of the North, “that she dried up quickly in the sun.
s.note: הִתְיַבֵּשׁ (hitpa'el) = to dry up, become dry, from יָבֵשׁ (dry). The pi'el יִבֵּשׁ = to dry something: לְיַבֵּשׁ כְּבִיסָה (to dry laundry). Hitpa'el often means "to become …" this way.

s.line: That is the end of her.
But the silver shoes are yours, and you shall have them to wear.”
s.note: שַׁיָּךְ לְ… = belongs to: לְמִי זֶה שַׁיָּךְ? (whose is this?). It agrees with the thing owned: נַעֲלַיִם is feminine plural, so שַׁיָּכוֹת. And again נָעַל is the verb for wearing shoes.

s.line: She reached down and picked up the shoes,
s.note: הֵרִים (hif'il of ר־ו־ם, the root of רָם, high) = to lift, pick up: הֵרִים אֶת הַטֵּלֵפוֹן (picked up the phone). הִתְכּוֹפֵף = to bend down, from כָּפַף (to bend).

s.line: and after shaking the dust out of them handed them to Dorothy.
“The Witch of the East was proud of those silver shoes,” said one of the Munchkins, “and there is some charm connected with them;
s.note: קָשׁוּר = tied, and also connected, related: זֶה לֹא קָשׁוּר (that's beside the point). It is the pa'ul participle of קָשַׁר (to tie). כִּשּׁוּף = a spell, sorcery, from the same root as מְכַשֵּׁפָה. גֵּאֶה בְּ… = proud of.

s.line: but what it is we never knew.”
Dorothy carried the shoes into the house and placed them on the table.
s.note: הִכְנִיס (hif'il) = to bring in, put in, the causative of נִכְנַס (to come in): נִכְנַסְתִּי = I came in, הִכְנַסְתִּי = I brought (something) in.

s.line: Then she came out again to the Munchkins and said:
“I am anxious to get back to my aunt and uncle, for I am sure they will worry about me.
s.note: דָּאַג לְ… means both "to worry about" and "to take care of": אַל תִּדְאַג = don't worry, אֲנִי אֶדְאַג לָזֶה = I'll take care of it. In chapter 1 Uncle Henry went לִדְאֹג לַבְּהֵמוֹת, to look after the animals.

s.line: Can you help me find my way?”
s.note: עָזַר לְ… = to help someone: the person takes לְ, not אֶת: אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲזֹר לְךָ? (can I help you?), what shop assistants say.

s.line: The Munchkins and the Witch first looked at one another, and then at Dorothy, and then shook their heads.
s.note: זֶה עַל זֶה = at each other; the preposition goes in the middle: זֶה עִם זֶה (with each other), זֶה לְזֶה (to each other). הֵנִיעַ אֶת הָרֹאשׁ בִּשְׁלִילָה = to shake one's head "no"; שְׁלִילָה = negation, from שָׁלַל (to rule out, deny).

w: וְאַף אֶחָד|and no one|~with לֹא: nobody
וּלְהִשָּׁאֵר בַּחַיִּים|and stay alive|~idiom: remain in life
s.line: “At the East, not far from here,” said one, “there is a great desert, and none could live to cross it.”
s.note: חָצָה = to cross, also to cut in half: לַחֲצוֹת אֶת הַכְּבִישׁ (to cross the road), and חֲצִי (half) is from the same root. נִשְׁאַר בַּחַיִּים = to survive, literally "to remain in life".

s.line: “It is the same at the South,” said another, “for I have been there and seen it.
The South is the country of the Quadlings.”
“I am told,” said the third man, “that it is the same at the West.
s.note: סִפְּרוּ לִי = "they told me", with no subject, the Hebrew way to say "I am told". As in chapter 1, a plural verb without a subject replaces the English passive.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: And that country, where the Winkies live, is ruled by the Wicked Witch of the West,
s.note: הַהִיא = "that" (fem.), pointing to something farther away; הַזֹּאת = "this". So בָּאֶרֶץ הַהִיא = in that country. The masculine is הַהוּא: בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא (on that day).

s.line: who would make you her slave if you passed her way.”
s.note: שִׁעְבֵּד (pi'el, four-letter root) = to enslave, related to עֶבֶד (slave). Again הָיָה + participle in both halves of an unreal "if" sentence: הִיא הָיְתָה מְשַׁעְבֶּדֶת … אִם הָיִית עוֹבֶרֶת.

s.line: “The North is my home,” said the old lady, “and at its edge is the same great desert that surrounds this Land of Oz.
s.note: הִקִּיף (hif'il) = to surround, encircle; מַקִּיף also means comprehensive: סֶקֶר מַקִּיף (a comprehensive survey). הֶקֵּף = circumference.

s.line: I’m afraid, my dear, you will have to live with us.”
s.note: אֲנִי חוֹשֶׁשֶׁת שֶׁ… = "I'm afraid that …", the polite way to give bad news, followed by the future. הִצְטָרֵךְ = to need to, have to; in hitpa'el the ת turns into ט after צ: תִּצְטָרְכִי, not *תִּתְצָרְכִי. יַקִּירָתִי = my dear (to a woman); to a man יַקִּירִי.

s.line: Dorothy began to sob at this, for she felt lonely among all these strange people.
s.note: הִרְגִּישׁ (hif'il) + adjective = to feel …: אֲנִי מַרְגִּישׁ טוֹב (I feel good). רֶגֶשׁ = a feeling. בּוֹדֵד = lonely, alone; בְּדִידוּת = loneliness.

w: נִרְאֶה שֶׁ|it seems that|~idiom: it looks that
s.line: Her tears seemed to grieve the kind-hearted Munchkins, for they immediately took out their handkerchiefs and began to weep also.
s.note: טוֹבֵי הַלֵּב = kind-hearted, an adjective in the construct with a noun, like טוֹב לֵב (sing.); also קְצַר רוּחַ (impatient). הֶעֱצִיב (hif'il) = to make sad, from עָצוּב (sad). נִרְאֶה שֶׁ… = it seems that ….

s.line: As for the little old woman, she took off her cap and balanced the point on the end of her nose,
s.note: וְאִלּוּ = whereas, as for, used to contrast two people: הוּא אוֹהֵב קָפֶה, וְאִלּוּ הִיא אוֹהֶבֶת תֵּה. On its own, אִלּוּ = "if" (unreal). אִזֵּן (pi'el) = to balance; אִזּוּן = balance, also a budget balance in the news.

s.line: while she counted “One, two, three” in a solemn voice.
s.note: סָפְרָה (pa'al) = she counted, not סִפְּרָה (she told). Israelis count with the feminine numbers אַחַת, שְׁתַּיִם, שָׁלוֹשׁ. חֲגִיגִי = festive or solemn, from חַג (holiday).

s.line: At once the cap changed to a slate, on which was written in big, white chalk marks:
s.note: הָפַךְ לְ… without an object = "turned into, became": הַחֲלוֹם הָפַךְ לִמְצִיאוּת (the dream became reality). כָּתוּב (pa'ul of כָּתַב) = written: מָה כָּתוּב פֹּה? (what does it say here?).

s.line: “LET DOROTHY GO TO THE CITY OF EMERALDS”
s.note: שֶׁ… + future = "let …, may …": שֶׁיִּכָּנֵס (let him come in), שֶׁיְּחַכֶּה (let him wait). It is how Hebrew gives a command to a third person.

s.line: The little old woman took the slate from her nose, and having read the words on it, asked,

w: קוֹרְאִים לָךְ|your name is|~idiom: (they) call you
s.line: “Is your name Dorothy, my dear?”
s.note: קוֹרְאִים לָךְ … = "they call you …", the normal way to talk about names: אֵיךְ קוֹרְאִים לְךָ? (what's your name?), קוֹרְאִים לִי דָּנָה (my name is Dana). Note that קָרְאָה in the sentence before means "read": the same verb means both "read" and "call".

w: וְהֵרִימָה מַבָּט|and looked up|~idiom: raised a look
s.line: “Yes,” answered the child, looking up and drying her tears.
s.note: הֵרִים מַבָּט = "raised a look", to look up; the opposite is הִשְׁפִּיל מַבָּט (to look down). נִגֵּב (pi'el) = to wipe, dry; מַגֶּבֶת = a towel.

s.line: “Then you must go to the City of Emeralds.
s.note: אִם כָּךְ = "if so, in that case", a little more formal than אָז. צָרִיךְ / צְרִיכָה + infinitive = must, need to.

s.line: Perhaps Oz will help you.”
“Where is this city?” asked Dorothy.
“It is exactly in the center of the country, and is ruled by Oz, the Great Wizard I told you of.”
s.note: וְשׁוֹלֵט בָּהּ אוֹז: Hebrew may put the verb before the subject, which lets "Oz" sit next to the description that follows it. שֶׁסִּפַּרְתִּי לָךְ עָלָיו = "that I told you about him": סִפֵּר עַל = to tell about, and the relative clause repeats the person as עָלָיו.

s.line: “Is he a good man?” inquired the girl anxiously.
s.note: A yes/no question in Hebrew is just a statement with a rising voice: <t>הוּא אָדָם טוֹב?</t> In writing the <t>?</t> does all the work. <t>אָדָם</t> = a person, a human being; <t>בִּדְאָגָה</t> = with worry, from <t>דָּאַג</t>.

s.line: “He is a good Wizard.
Whether he is a man or not I cannot tell, for I have never seen him.”
s.note: אִם means both "if" and "whether": אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ אִם הוּא בָּא (I don't know whether he's coming). Putting אֶת זֶה first stresses it: "that I can't say".

s.line: “How can I get there?” asked Dorothy.
“You must walk.
s.note: בָּרֶגֶל = on foot: הָלַכְנוּ בָּרֶגֶל (we walked). הוֹלֵךְ רֶגֶל = a pedestrian.

s.line: It is a long journey, through a country that is sometimes pleasant and sometimes dark and terrible.
s.note: מַסָּע = a journey, a trek; נָסַע = to travel, from the same root. דֶּרֶךְ = way, road, and before a place it means "via, through": טָסְנוּ דֶּרֶךְ רוֹמָא (we flew via Rome).

s.line: However, I will use all the magic arts I know of to keep you from harm.”
s.note: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ… = to use; note the בְּ: אֲנִי מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּמַּחְשֵׁב. In hitpa'el the ת swaps places with a first letter שׁ: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ, not *הִתְשַׁמֵּשׁ. שָׁמַר עַל = to look after, protect. עִם זֹאת = however, nevertheless, typical of written Hebrew.

s.line: “Won’t you go with me?” pleaded the girl, who had begun to look upon the little old woman as her only friend.
s.note: רָאָה בְּ־X אֶת Y = to see X as Y, regard X as Y: הוּא רוֹאֶה בָּהּ אֶת הַיּוֹרֶשֶׁת שֶׁלּוֹ (he sees her as his successor). הִתְחַנֵּן (hitpa'el) = to beg, plead; חֵן (grace, charm) shares the root.

s.line: “No, I cannot do that,” she replied, “but I will give you my kiss,

w: וְאַף אֶחָד|and no one|~with לֹא: nobody
s.line: and no one will dare injure a person who has been kissed by the Witch of the North.”
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ… = to hurt, harm, hit (a target): לֹא הִתְכַּוַּנְתִּי לִפְגֹּעַ בְּךָ (I didn't mean to hurt you). Its nif'al נִפְגַּע = was hurt, as at the start of the chapter. הֵעֵז = to dare; עַז = strong, bold. "Who has been kissed" becomes active: "who got a kiss".

s.line: She came close to Dorothy and kissed her gently on the forehead.
s.note: נָשַׁק לְ… (pa'al) = to kiss, with לְ; in speech the pi'el נִשֵּׁק is just as common: הוּא נִשֵּׁק אוֹתָהּ. נְשִׁיקָה = a kiss.

s.line: Where her lips touched the girl they left a round, shining mark,
s.note: בַּמָּקוֹם שֶׁבּוֹ = "in the place in which", that is, where. שְׂפָתַיִם is feminine, so "they" is הֵן. שָׂפָה also means a language: שְׂפַת אֵם = mother tongue.

s.line: as Dorothy found out soon after.
s.note: גִּלָּה (pi'el) = to discover, find out; תַּגְלִית = a discovery. The nif'al נִגְלָה = was revealed.

s.line: “The road to the City of Emeralds is paved with yellow brick,” said the Witch, “so you cannot miss it.
s.note: רָצוּף = paved, covered (a pa'ul form from the root of רִצְפָּה, floor), and also "continuous": שָׁלוֹשׁ שָׁנִים רְצוּפוֹת (three years in a row). The proverb: הַדֶּרֶךְ לַגֵּיהִנֹּם רְצוּפָה כַּוָּנוֹת טוֹבוֹת. פִּסְפֵס = to miss (a chance, a bus, a turn), everyday spoken Hebrew.

s.line: When you get to Oz do not be afraid of him, but tell your story and ask him to help you.
s.note: כְּשֶׁ… about the future takes the future: כְּשֶׁתַּגִּיעִי = "when you (will) get". "Don't …" is אַל + future: אַל תְּפַחֲדִי. אֶלָּא = "but rather", only after a negative. בִּקֵּשׁ מִ… = to ask someone (for something).

s.line: Good-bye, my dear.”
s.note: לְהִתְרָאוֹת = good-bye, literally "to see each other (again)": a hitpa'el infinitive of רָאָה, with the "each other" meaning of hitpa'el.

w: דֶּרֶךְ צְלֵחָה|a good journey|~idiom: a successful road
s.line: The three Munchkins bowed low to her and wished her a pleasant journey,
s.note: שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַ… is the construct form of the number: "the three …": שְׁלוֹשֶׁת הַיְּלָדִים (the three children). דֶּרֶךְ צְלֵחָה! = bon voyage. אִחֵל (pi'el) = to wish someone something; אִחוּלִים = good wishes.

s.line: after which they walked away through the trees.
s.note: הִתְרַחֵק (hitpa'el) = to move away, from רָחוֹק (far); its opposite הִתְקָרֵב (to come near) appeared earlier in the chapter.

s.line: The Witch gave Dorothy a friendly little nod, whirled around on her left heel three times, and straightway disappeared,
s.note: עָקֵב = heel. With other vowels, עֵקֶב = "due to", a formal word heard on the news: הַטִּיסָה בֻּטְּלָה עֵקֶב מֶזֶג הָאֲוִיר (the flight was cancelled due to the weather). הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn around, also "to wander around": הִסְתּוֹבַבְנוּ בָּעִיר.

s.line: much to the surprise of little Toto,
s.note: הֻפְתַּע is hof'al, the passive of the hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (to surprise): הִיא הִפְתִּיעָה אוֹתוֹ → הוּא הֻפְתַּע. הַפְתָּעָה = a surprise, and מַפְתִּיעַ = surprising.

w: בְּקוֹל רָם|loudly|~lit. in a high voice
s.line: who barked after her loudly enough when she had gone, because he had been afraid even to growl while she stood by.
s.note: כָּל זְמַן שֶׁ… = as long as, all the while: כָּל זְמַן שֶׁאַתָּה פֹּה (as long as you're here). לְמַדַּי = quite, enough, a written word; in speech דֵּי before the adjective. לְיָדוֹ = next to him, from יָד (hand).

s.line: But Dorothy, knowing her to be a witch, had expected her to disappear in just that way,
s.note: Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought: Dorothy expected "she will disappear", so <t>צִפְּתָה שֶׁהִיא תֵּעָלֵם</t>. <t>תֵּעָלֵם</t> is the nif'al future of <t>נֶעֱלַם</t>. <t>כָּכָה</t> = like this, so, the spoken form of <t>כָּךְ</t>.

s.line: and was not surprised in the least.
